Pervious means allowing something — usually a liquid or gas — to pass through.

If a material is pervious, it has tiny gaps, holes, or pores in it, and things like water or air can move through those gaps from one side to the other.

The easiest way to lock in this meaning is through its much more famous opposite: impervious. You've almost certainly seen that word. Something impervious blocks everything — nothing gets in, nothing passes through. Pervious is simply the flip side of that coin. Where impervious means "no passage," pervious means "passage is allowed."
What It Looks Like in the Real World

Think about two different surfaces after it rains:

  • A parking lot paved with regular asphalt: water pools on the surface and runs off to the side. It has nowhere to go because the asphalt is tightly packed. That surface is not pervious.
  • A gravel path or a lawn: rainwater sinks right into the ground. The gaps between soil particles or gravel pieces let the water travel downward. That surface is pervious.

More examples:

  • Sandy soil is pervious — pour water on it and it disappears into the ground quickly.
  • Clay soil is far less pervious — it's tightly packed, so water sits on top or drains very slowly.
  • A sponge is pervious — water moves straight through it.
  • A sheet of glass is not pervious — water cannot pass through it at all.
Where You'll Mostly Encounter This Word

"Pervious" is not an everyday conversational word. You'll encounter it mainly in technical and professional fields:

Civil engineering and urban planning: Engineers talk about "pervious pavement" or "pervious concrete" — specially designed road and sidewalk surfaces that let rainwater drain down through the material into the ground below, rather than flooding streets or overwhelming drainage systems. This is a major real-world application of the word.

Geology and hydrology (the study of water): Scientists describe rock and soil layers as pervious or impervious depending on whether water can flow through them. This matters enormously for understanding underground water supplies (aquifers), predicting floods, and managing irrigation.

Environmental science: Whether a surface is pervious or not affects how much rainwater replenishes underground water reserves vs. how much flows into rivers as runoff (sometimes carrying pollutants with it).
A Subtle but Important Point: Degree

"Pervious" isn't always all-or-nothing. Materials can be more or less pervious. A rock with lots of cracks is more pervious than a dense rock with few cracks. You'll sometimes see comparisons like:

"Limestone is more pervious than granite."

This means water can travel through limestone more easily than through granite, even though neither is as pervious as loose gravel.

In older or formal writing, you may occasionally see "pervious" used in a non-physical sense, meaning open or receptive to influence, reason, or argument. For example:

"She was pervious to new ideas and always willing to change her mind."

This figurative usage maps the same core logic: just as a pervious material lets water through, a pervious mind lets ideas or persuasion through. However, this figurative sense is uncommon in modern English. If you see "pervious" today, assume it's about physical passage unless the context clearly suggests otherwise.
Words That Mean the Same Thing

These are close synonyms — words you can often swap in:

  • Permeable — the most direct synonym; used very widely in science. Permeable and pervious are nearly interchangeable in most contexts.
  • Porous — technically means "full of pores or holes," but in practice it's used similarly. The slight difference: porous emphasizes the presence of holes; pervious emphasizes that passage through those holes is possible. In everyday use, however, the distinction rarely matters.
How to Use It in Sentences

• "The engineers replaced the old concrete with a pervious material so that stormwater could drain naturally."
  • "That layer of rock is pervious, which means water from the surface can slowly filter down to the aquifer beneath it."
  • "Unlike the clay-rich soil nearby, the sandy ground here is highly pervious."
  • "Pervious pavements reduce flooding by allowing rainwater to seep into the earth instead of running off into drains."

Pervious = able to be passed through (especially by water or other fluids). It is the direct opposite of impervious, and it describes materials with gaps or pores that allow liquids or gases to travel through them. It lives mostly in technical fields like engineering, geology, and environmental science, where whether water can move through a surface or not is a critical question.
